items.title: L15: Testing an exception to open competition
items.body: The Recruitment Principles allow some appointments without open competition, but an exception is a tool for a stated purpose, not a shortcut. A sound test has four questions. First, does the situation genuinely fall within a recognised exception, such as a short-term appointment to meet a temporary need, a secondment or loan, or a scheme designed to help a defined group into work? Second, is the reason one the exception was designed for, and not simply that a competition would be slower or less certain? Third, are the limits observed: time limits on short-term appointments, the requirement that the appointee is not simply carried into a permanent post, and any approvals the department's own policy requires? Fourth, is the decision recorded, with reasons that someone else could audit? An exception that fails any of these can breach the Principles even when the appointee is excellent. Quality of the person is not a justification for avoiding competition, because the principle protects the opportunity of others to apply. Repeated reliance on short-term appointments to cover a permanent need, successive extensions beyond the permitted period and use of a secondment as a back door into a permanent post are the common patterns the Commission examines. Where an exception genuinely applies and then the need becomes permanent, the usual route is to advertise the permanent post and let the incumbent compete with everyone else. Departments should be able to explain why open competition could not be used, what safeguards applied and how the arrangement ended. If uncertain, a department asks HR or the Commission before making the appointment, rather than defending it afterwards.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to appoint an excellent contractor straight into a permanent post because a competition would take months. Which analysis is correct?

options.text: A short delay is a recognised exception provided the manager records the reason
Speed and the person's quality are not valid grounds, so the post needs open competition
A contractor counts as a civil servant, so no competition is needed
An excellent person justifies an exception, as merit is the central principle

questions.hint: Convenience and quality do not create an exception.

questions.prompt: Which pair of facts is most likely to justify a genuine exception?

options.text: A tight timetable and a preference for continuity in the team
A wish to avoid disappointing applicants and a fixed budget
A time-limited need to cover maternity leave and a clear end date
A strong candidate already known to the team and a long-term need

questions.hint: A temporary need with limits fits a short-term exception.

questions.prompt: A short-term appointment has been extended several times beyond the usual limit without approval. What is the main concern?

options.text: It means that the appointee has a right to a permanent post
It means the department has saved on recruitment costs
It shows that the original appointment was invalid from the outset
It may be using an exception to avoid competition for a permanent need

questions.hint: Repeated extension can become a back door.

questions.prompt: When a temporary need becomes permanent, what is usually the correct step?

options.text: Advertise the permanent post and let the incumbent compete with others
Ask the incumbent's manager to confirm the appointment
Convert the incumbent to permanent status after a review
Extend the exception for a further period while a decision is made

questions.prompt: Why is the quality of the appointee not a justification for bypassing competition?

options.text: The principle protects the chance of others to apply, whatever the appointee's merit
Quality can be assessed only by a formal competition
Appointees from outside the Civil Service cannot be assessed otherwise
Excellent people are always willing to compete

questions.prompt: Which record would best support an exception if audited?

options.text: A note of the candidate's salary and start date
A record of the number of applications that would have been expected
The reason the exception applied, why competition was not used and the limits observed
A note that the candidate was well regarded by the team

questions.hint: Recorded reasons make the decision auditable.

questions.prompt: A department is unsure whether an exception applies. What should it do before making the appointment?

options.text: Offer the post to the candidate and gather evidence later
Ask HR or the Commission for advice, rather than defend it afterwards
Make the appointment and seek approval if challenged
Treat it as an exception because it is urgent

questions.prompt: Which situation is a common pattern of misuse?

options.text: Using a loan to share expertise between two departments
Using a short-term appointment to cover a known absence
Using a secondment to give an employee experience in another organisation
Using a secondment as a route into a permanent post without competition

questions.hint: Secondment as back door is a pattern.

questions.prompt: Which question is NOT part of a sound test of an exception?

options.text: Whether the situation falls within a recognised exception
Whether the decision has been recorded with reasons
Whether the manager prefers the person concerned
Whether time limits and approvals have been observed

questions.prompt: What should a department be able to explain about an exception?

options.text: Why open competition could not be used, what safeguards applied and how it ended
Why the exception was approved in the previous year
Why the appointee was the most popular candidate
Why the appointee's pay was set at its level

items.title: L15: Weighing evidence from outside the Civil Service
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: Panels increasingly assess candidates from other sectors, such as local government, the private sector, charities and the armed forces, alongside existing civil servants. Fair assessment means judging each person's evidence on its merits against the criteria, not against a template of Civil Service experience. The risks are two-sided. A panel may undervalue evidence that uses unfamiliar terms or contexts, for example scoring a business leader who describes profit, customers and contracts below a civil servant who describes ministers, submissions and parliamentary questions. Equally, a panel may overvalue impressive-sounding backgrounds without testing whether the evidence shows the behaviour at the required level. Good practice is to define in advance what each criterion requires in terms of actions and outcomes, and to score the evidence of actions and outcomes, whatever the setting. A question about Making Effective Decisions asks what you decided, on what information, with what risk and with what result, and it can be answered in any sector. Panels should be briefed to look past vocabulary, to ask neutral follow-up questions, and to avoid assuming that civil service context is necessary where it is not. Candidates from outside government should explain context briefly, translate jargon, and show how their evidence relates to the criteria; civil servants should avoid relying on internal shorthand. Where a post genuinely needs knowledge of government, such as the machinery of government or parliamentary process, the advert should say so and the criterion should be assessed explicitly, rather than assumed. This approach supports fair and open competition because it treats evidence consistently across backgrounds.

questions.prompt: A panel scores a business leader's evidence lower because it is about customers and contracts, not ministers. What is the problem?

options.text: It follows the rule that internal candidates must be preferred
It rates vocabulary and setting instead of the actions and outcomes the criterion requires
It correctly reflects the need for government experience in every post
It reflects the fact that business evidence is always less complex

questions.hint: Score actions and outcomes, not setting.

questions.prompt: What is the opposite risk when assessing outside candidates?

options.text: Treating all private sector evidence as irrelevant
Placing them automatically on a reserve list
Giving them no interview at all
Overvaluing impressive-sounding backgrounds without testing the evidence

questions.prompt: How can a panel prepare to assess evidence fairly across sectors?

options.text: Score according to the seniority of the candidate's last title
Agree that civil service examples will carry more weight
Define in advance what each criterion requires in actions and outcomes
Ask each candidate to translate every term before scoring

questions.prompt: Which neutral follow-up question is most useful to a panel?

options.text: What did you personally decide and what was the result?
Why did you not use the Civil Service approach?
Who else was involved who works in government?
How would a civil servant have handled it?

questions.hint: Neutral questions seek action and outcome.

questions.prompt: What should an outside candidate do to help the panel?

options.text: Use as much sector jargon as possible to show expertise
Avoid mentioning their sector to avoid confusing the panel
Leave out outcomes that cannot be compared with government
Explain context briefly, translate jargon and link evidence to the criteria

questions.prompt: What should a serving civil servant avoid?

options.text: Quantifying outcomes where possible
Relying on internal shorthand that outsiders and some scorers may not know
Linking examples to the criteria
Describing their own contribution in the first person

questions.prompt: A post requires knowledge of parliamentary process. How should this be handled?

options.text: The advert should state it and the criterion should be assessed explicitly
It should be tested only on candidates from outside government
It should be scored through length of service
It should be assumed for all candidates and left unassessed

questions.prompt: Why does consistent treatment of evidence across backgrounds matter?

options.text: It means that all candidates pass the sift
It guarantees that outside candidates are appointed in proportion to their numbers
It removes the need for interviews
It supports fair and open competition on merit

questions.prompt: What does a question about Making Effective Decisions ask, in any sector?

options.text: Which decisions were approved by ministers
What was decided, on what information, with what risk and with what result
How many decisions were taken in a year
Whether the candidate has made a decision under a government rule

questions.prompt: Which panel briefing most supports fairness to outside applicants?

options.text: Give outside applicants a lower pass mark
Prefer examples that mention familiar departments
Look past vocabulary and avoid assuming civil service context is necessary where it is not
Assess outside applicants separately from civil servants

items.title: L15: A colleague on loan applying to the host
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: A person on loan or secondment often develops strong evidence in the host and may want to apply for a permanent post there. This is allowed, but it raises fairness issues that the host and the individual must manage. First, eligibility: the advert must be open to the person. If it is restricted to the host department's staff, a person on loan from another department may not be eligible, and the host may not simply widen it for one person. Second, impartiality: the person has been working with the panel's colleagues and may be known to panel members. Panel members should declare their relationship, and anyone who has line-managed the candidate or who has a close working relationship may need to stand down or be balanced by independent members. Third, information: the person may know details of the post, the budget, the team's plans and other candidates that outsiders do not. They should not use confidential information in their application, and should not take part in designing the role or the criteria. Fourth, evidence: the panel should assess the person on the same criteria as others, using evidence of what they have done, not on an impression of how well they fit in. Fifth, expectations: the host manager should not suggest that the post is for the person on loan, and the lending department should be informed so that their return plan is not undermined. If the person is not successful, they should return to their home post with their evidence and feedback. If the host wants to keep the person while the post is advertised, a short extension of the loan with a clear end date may be appropriate, but the host should not create a long-running arrangement that makes the person the obvious candidate.

questions.prompt: A person on loan from another department wants to apply for a host post restricted to host staff. What is the correct position?

options.text: They are eligible if the lending department consents
They are eligible because they currently work in the host
They are eligible if the host manager agrees
They are probably ineligible and the host should not widen the advert for one person

questions.hint: Eligibility follows the advert, not the individual.

questions.prompt: What should happen if the panel includes the person's host line manager?

options.text: The manager should chair the panel because they know the work
The manager should give the panel a summary of the candidate's performance
The manager should declare the relationship and may need to stand down or be balanced by independent members
The manager should score the candidate first

questions.prompt: Which action by the person on loan would be improper?

options.text: Helping to design the criteria for the post they intend to apply for
Asking for feedback after the process
Declaring their relationship with panel members
Preparing their application using their own work evidence

questions.prompt: Why must the person not use confidential information in their application?

options.text: It would be unlikely to be believed by the panel
Other candidates would not have it, which would make the competition unfair
It is simply poor style
It would breach their contract with the lending department only

questions.prompt: How should the panel assess the person?

options.text: By the host manager's description of their work
Against the same criteria, using evidence of what they have done
By their fit with the host team
By the number of months they have been on loan

questions.prompt: What should the host manager avoid?

options.text: Telling the lending department about the application
Giving the person feedback on their loan work
Suggesting that the post is intended for the person on loan
Encouraging the person to consider applying

questions.prompt: Why should the lending department be informed of the application?

options.text: Because the lender must approve the application
Because the lender sets the closing date
Because the lender scores the application
So that the person's return plan is not undermined and the lender can plan

questions.hint: Lenders need to plan for return.

questions.prompt: If the loan expires before the competition ends, what is the usual approach?

options.text: A short extension with a clear end date may be appropriate
An immediate permanent appointment pending the outcome
A long extension until the post is filled whatever the time
A new loan with no end date

questions.prompt: What risk arises if the host keeps the person on loan for a long time before advertising the post?

options.text: The post will be regraded
The lending department will cancel the loan
The person may become the obvious candidate, undermining fair and open competition
The person will lose their right to apply

questions.prompt: The person on loan is unsuccessful. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Return to the home post with the evidence and feedback gained
Accept a lower-grade post in the host
Raise a formal complaint about the competition
Remain in the host indefinitely as an acting appointee

items.title: L15: Chairing a panel and managing a difficult candidate or colleague
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; departmental recruitment guidance
items.body: The panel chair carries the responsibility for the fairness of the process. Before the competition begins, the chair should check that every member understands the criteria, the scoring guide and their duty to declare interests. During assessment, the chair keeps to the timetable, ensures candidates are treated consistently, and prevents any member from dominating. Difficult moments arise. A panel member may express a view early that shapes the others, so the chair should encourage independent scoring before discussion. A member may ask irrelevant questions about family plans, age or health, which could lead to discrimination, and the chair should stop them and, if needed, record the incident. A candidate may become distressed or ask for a break, in which case the chair should respond with reasonable flexibility, within the agreed adjustments. A candidate may raise a complaint during the interview, and the chair should listen, record it, and refer it to HR afterwards without making promises. If a member realises that a candidate is a friend, the chair should consider whether the member should withdraw, and whether the candidate should be told. The chair makes sure that scores are justified by notes, resolves differences by returning to evidence and not by seniority, and avoids a compromise score that no one believes. After the decision, the chair ensures that feedback is consistent and that records are kept. If the chair believes that the process has been compromised, for example by a member who has leaked information, the chair should report it at once and take advice on whether the competition can continue. The chair should also be aware of their own bias and invite challenge.

questions.prompt: A panel member states early in the discussion that candidate B is clearly best. What should the chair do?

options.text: Tell the member to stay silent in future
Encourage independent scoring on the evidence before further discussion
Allow the senior member's view to lead the discussion
Average the scores of the remaining members

questions.prompt: A panel member asks a candidate about their plans to have children. What should the chair do?

options.text: Ask the candidate to reply anyway
Allow the question if the candidate does not object
Ignore the question to avoid embarrassment
Stop the line of questioning and record the incident

questions.prompt: A candidate becomes distressed. How should the chair respond?

options.text: By asking the candidate to leave and reapply later
With reasonable flexibility within the agreed adjustments, such as offering a short break
By continuing without comment to protect fairness
By ending the interview and recording a zero score

questions.prompt: A candidate complains about the process during the interview. What should the chair do?

options.text: Listen, record it and refer it to HR afterwards without promises
Pause the interview and invite other candidates to comment
Dismiss the complaint as out of order
Promise to change the scores

questions.prompt: A panel member realises that a candidate is a friend. What is the chair's responsibility?

options.text: Ignore it if the friend is not a close one
Ask the candidate to withdraw
Consider whether the member should withdraw and whether the candidate should be told
Ask the member to score the candidate lightly

questions.prompt: How should the chair resolve a difference of scores between two members?

options.text: By accepting the senior member's score
By asking the candidate for further evidence
By using the average of the two
By returning to the notes and evidence

questions.prompt: Why should the chair avoid a compromise score that no one believes?

options.text: It lowers the candidate's score unfairly
It disconnects the score from the evidence and weakens the record
It is prohibited by the Equality Act
It makes the interview last longer

questions.prompt: A member leaks information about the competition. What should the chair do?

options.text: Wait until the end and see whether it affected the outcome
Remove the leaked information from the records
Warn the member informally
Report it at once and take advice on whether the competition can continue

questions.prompt: What should the chair do after the decision?

options.text: Publish the scores to all applicants
Destroy the notes to protect candidates
Ensure feedback is consistent and records are kept
Allow members to give their own feedback to candidates

questions.prompt: Why should the chair invite challenge to their own views?

options.text: Everyone is subject to bias, and openness protects the fairness of the process
Because chairs are not allowed to score
Because the chair's view carries no weight
Because panels should have no leader

items.title: L15: What diversity monitoring data can and cannot show
items.source: Equality Act 2010; Civil Service Commission; Civil Service diversity reporting
items.body: Departments collect data on the diversity of applicants and successful candidates at each stage, such as sift, test, interview and appointment, with the aim of spotting patterns that might indicate barriers. Candidates are usually asked to provide this information voluntarily on a form kept separate from their application, and it is not seen by the panel. The data is used in aggregate and handled under data protection law. Used carefully, it can show where a group is dropping out disproportionately, for example at a particular test or at sift, and so prompt a review of a criterion, a question or a practice. It cannot, by itself, prove discrimination. Differences in outcome can arise from many factors, such as the profile of applicants, experience and chance, particularly with small numbers, where percentages can swing sharply. Statistical caution is needed: a drop from three successful out of ten applicants to two out of ten is not a meaningful pattern. To be useful, data should be compared over time and across competitions, with enough numbers, and followed up by qualitative review such as reading a sample of sift decisions for consistency. Responses should be proportionate: change a test that appears to disadvantage a group without a job-related reason, widen advertising, review the panel's training, or add reasonable adjustments. Data must never be used to select or reject individuals on the basis of a protected characteristic. A department that reviews its data and acts is better able to show that it is meeting its duties, including the public sector equality duty. As a candidate, completing the form helps the department improve, and your answers do not affect your application.

questions.prompt: Who normally sees an individual candidate's diversity monitoring form?

options.text: All other candidates
The panel members, to help them score fairly
Not the panel, as it is kept separate from the application
The candidate's line manager

questions.hint: The form is kept separate from assessment.

questions.prompt: What is the main use of the data?

options.text: To decide pay on appointment
To spot patterns in aggregate that may indicate barriers at a stage
To select candidates by protected characteristic
To rank departments by size

questions.prompt: Does a difference in outcomes between groups prove discrimination?

options.text: It does if the panel is not diverse
It does if the group is larger
It does, whatever the numbers
It does not by itself, as several factors can explain differences

questions.prompt: Why is caution needed when numbers are small?

options.text: Percentages can swing sharply on very small changes
Small numbers are exempt from the Equality Act
Small numbers show the biggest patterns
Small numbers are always accurate

questions.prompt: Which follow-up makes the data more useful?

options.text: Publishing individual results
Ignoring the data until a complaint arrives
Comparing across competitions and over time, and reading a sample of decisions
Changing the scores of affected candidates

questions.prompt: Which response to a pattern is proportionate?

options.text: Reviewing a test that appears to disadvantage a group without a job-related reason
Adjusting the scores of the affected group
Reducing the number of stages for everyone
Refusing to publish the data

questions.hint: Fix the practice, not the scores.

questions.prompt: What must data never be used for?

options.text: Reporting in aggregate to the Commission
Selecting or rejecting individuals on the basis of a protected characteristic
Training panel members
Reviewing a department's processes

questions.hint: Individual decisions must be on merit.

questions.prompt: How does reviewing and acting on the data help a department?

options.text: It removes the need for panel training
It allows the department to skip adjustments
It guarantees no complaint will succeed
It helps show it is meeting its duties, including the public sector equality duty

questions.prompt: How does completing the form affect your application?

options.text: It does not affect your application and helps the department improve
It decides whether you are shortlisted
It is passed to your line manager
It gives you extra marks

questions.prompt: A drop from three successes out of ten to two out of ten is observed. What is the right reading?

options.text: It proves a barrier has appeared
It proves that the panel has changed
It is not a meaningful pattern with numbers so small
It shows the department should stop collecting data

items.title: L15: Designing a fair promotion process for your own team
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: A senior manager who has a vacancy at the grade above must make several decisions that shape fairness before a single application arrives. First, decide the route: if the post is permanent, it must be filled through fair and open competition, usually advertised on Civil Service Jobs, and the scope of eligibility, such as department only or across government, should reflect the real need and not a preferred candidate. Second, define the criteria from the Success Profile for the post, selecting the elements and the stages that will be used and avoiding criteria that cannot be justified by the job, such as a specific type of experience that only one person has. Third, plan the assessment: decide the stages, scoring guide and pass marks in advance, brief the panel, and ensure the panel is balanced and includes someone independent. Fourth, communicate: advertise the vacancy to all eligible staff, including those who are absent, on part-time or flexible working patterns or on loan, and allow enough time. Fifth, manage conflicts: declare relationships, keep out of the sift if you have a strong view, and avoid giving any candidate privileged information. Sixth, deal with the acting-up question: if someone is acting in the post, set an end date and do not let the arrangement determine the outcome. Seventh, offer feedback to all candidates and record decisions with reasons. If the post is urgent, a short-term acting arrangement can bridge the gap, but it should be time limited and should not be a way to select a successor. A manager who follows these steps protects the candidates, the department and themselves, and signals that progression depends on merit.

questions.prompt: What determines how a permanent post at the grade above must be filled?

options.text: It can be filled by the manager choosing the best person
It must be filled through fair and open competition
It can be filled by the acting person automatically
It can be filled by agreement with the trade union

questions.prompt: How should the scope of eligibility be set?

options.text: To match the person the manager has in mind
To exclude staff on part-time hours
To keep the competition within the team
To reflect the real need and not a preferred candidate

questions.prompt: Which criterion would be hard to justify?

options.text: Evidence of managing a budget of the right size
A specific type of experience that only one person in the team has

A qualification that the job genuinely requires

questions.prompt: What should be decided before applications arrive?

options.text: The salary of the appointee
The names of the candidates to be interviewed
The stages, scoring guide and pass marks
The ranking of the staff in the team

questions.prompt: Who should be informed of the vacancy?

options.text: All eligible staff, including those absent, part time or on loan
Only those the manager thinks suitable
Only those with a recent appraisal rating of high
Only staff who are in the office

questions.hint: Openness includes people who are away.

questions.prompt: A manager has a strong view about a candidate. What should they do?

options.text: Lead the sift to ensure the right person progresses
Give the candidate extra help before the interview
Brief the panel on the candidate's strengths
Keep out of the sift and declare any relationship

questions.prompt: Someone is acting in the post. What should the manager do?

options.text: Extend the arrangement until the post is filled whatever the time
Tell the acting person the post is theirs
Appoint the acting person permanently after six months
Set an end date and not let the arrangement determine the outcome

questions.hint: Acting up should not decide the competition.

questions.prompt: If a post is urgent, what is an appropriate bridge?

options.text: An informal agreement to be confirmed later
A time-limited acting arrangement that does not select a successor
A permanent appointment without competition
A temporary promotion with no end date

questions.prompt: What should be given to all candidates after the decision?

options.text: The scores of other candidates
A report on the panel's views
Feedback, with decisions recorded with reasons

questions.prompt: Why does following these steps protect the manager?

options.text: It shows that progression depends on merit and that the process was fair
It removes the need for HR advice
It guarantees the manager's preferred candidate will win
It means complaints cannot be made

items.title: L15: Remedying a flawed competition
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: Sometimes a department discovers that a competition was flawed: a panel member had an undeclared relationship, a criterion was misapplied, scores were transposed, or an advert was inaccurate. The right response depends on the nature and effect of the flaw, and the department should decide it openly, with advice from HR. First, establish the facts: what happened, whom it affected and whether it could have changed the outcome. Second, decide whether the flaw is correctable. A calculation error that changes a ranking can usually be corrected by re-scoring and, where it changes who passes, informing affected candidates. A conflict of interest may be remedied by re-scoring with an independent panel member, provided the original records are sound. A serious flaw, such as pre-selection or an advert that excluded eligible people, may require the competition to be cancelled and re-run. Third, consider the candidates: those who were wrongly rejected should be given the opportunity to be reconsidered, and those already appointed should be dealt with fairly, which may include an agreed process and honest communication about the risks. Fourth, record the decision and reasons. Fifth, learn: identify why the flaw occurred and change the process, training or checks. The department may need to tell the Commission where the flaw involved a breach of the Principles. A department should avoid two errors: covering up a mistake, which damages trust and may be a breach in itself, and over-correcting by cancelling a competition where a simple fix would do. Honest and prompt action protects candidates and the department.

questions.prompt: Which flaw can usually be corrected by re-scoring?

options.text: Pre-selection of a candidate before the advert
A panel that had no independent member
An advert that excluded eligible staff
A calculation error that changed a ranking

questions.prompt: Which flaw may require the competition to be cancelled and re-run?

options.text: A mistake in a date on a letter
A candidate who arrived late
Pre-selection or an advert that excluded eligible people
A scorer who gave a low mark

questions.prompt: What is the first step on discovering a flaw?

options.text: Establish the facts, whom it affected and whether it could have changed the outcome
Inform the press
Offer the post to the runner-up
Dismiss the panel

questions.prompt: A conflict of interest is found and the original records are sound. What may be a proportionate remedy?

options.text: Appointing the candidate whose scores were affected
Re-scoring with an independent panel member
Cancelling every competition in the department

questions.prompt: What should happen for candidates who were wrongly rejected?

options.text: They should be told nothing
They should be compensated automatically
They should be given the chance to be reconsidered

questions.prompt: What is the risk for a candidate already appointed in a flawed competition?

options.text: They will lose their post at once
Their appointment may be affected, so they should be treated fairly and told honestly
They are protected from any action
They must repay their salary

questions.prompt: Which error should a department avoid?

options.text: Covering up a mistake, which damages trust and may be a breach in itself
Reporting the mistake to HR
Recording the reasons for its decision
Learning from the incident

questions.prompt: Which opposite error should it also avoid?

options.text: Seeking HR advice
Fixing a small mistake quickly
Informing the affected candidates
Over-correcting by cancelling a competition where a simple fix would do

questions.prompt: Why should the department record its decision and reasons?

options.text: To show that it acted openly and fairly and to support later review
To allow the decision to be changed later without notice
To provide material for the press
To avoid telling candidates the outcome

questions.prompt: Why might the department tell the Commission?

options.text: Because the Commission appoints the replacement panel
Where the flaw involved a breach of the Principles

Because every flaw must be reported within a day

items.title: L15: Reviews, appeals and complaints compared
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; ACAS guidance
items.body: People use the words review, appeal and complaint loosely, but in a recruitment setting they have different meanings and routes. A request for feedback is not a challenge: it asks the panel to explain how you were assessed. A review or reconsideration asks the department to check whether a decision was made correctly, for example whether scores were added up properly or a criterion was applied as intended. Some departments offer a review for a limited set of grounds, such as procedural errors, and not for a disagreement with the panel's judgement. A complaint under the Recruitment Principles asserts that the process breached the Principles, such as an unadvertised vacancy or an undeclared conflict, and follows the department's complaints process and then, if needed, the Commission. A grievance is an employment process for a current employee who has a workplace issue, including how they were treated in a competition. A claim of discrimination in recruitment can be taken to an employment tribunal within a short time limit, usually counted from the date of the act, and early conciliation through ACAS is normally required before a claim. These routes can run side by side, but they have different aims, evidence and time limits. A review seeks to correct, a complaint seeks a finding of breach, a grievance seeks resolution of a workplace issue, and a tribunal claim seeks a legal remedy. Before choosing a route, identify what you want: an explanation, a corrected score, an apology, a change of practice or a legal remedy. Seek advice from a trade union representative, HR or ACAS, keep dates, and be careful about time limits, which can expire quickly.

questions.prompt: Which route asks a panel to explain how you were assessed?

options.text: A grievance
A tribunal claim
A complaint under the Recruitment Principles
A request for feedback

questions.hint: Feedback explains, it does not challenge.

questions.prompt: What does a review or reconsideration normally ask?

options.text: That the department pay compensation
That the department change its mind because you disagree
That the department check whether the decision was made correctly, such as scores added up properly
That the department apply a different set of criteria

questions.prompt: On which grounds do some departments allow review?

options.text: A limited set such as procedural error, not mere disagreement with judgement
Only the final score
Only discrimination
Any ground the candidate raises

questions.prompt: What does a complaint under the Recruitment Principles assert?

items.title: L15: Civil Service Code dilemmas in a job search
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code
items.body: A career move can raise conduct questions that a civil servant should recognise. Suppose a supplier or partner you deal with in your job offers to introduce you to a vacancy or hints that a job could be available. Accepting would create a conflict of interest, because your decisions about the supplier could be, or appear to be, influenced by your hopes of a job. The right step is to tell your line manager, declare the discussion and remove yourself from decisions about that organisation, and the Code's values of integrity and impartiality apply. Similarly, if you are offered hospitality or a gift by a potential employer in the course of your work, follow the department's rules, which normally require declaration and often refusal. If you are thinking of leaving to join an outside body, the business appointment rules require civil servants to seek approval for certain appointments, with greater scrutiny for senior roles and for work connected with your official duties, and departments usually decide for more junior staff. You must not use official information, contacts or time to prepare an outside application, and you must not take documents with you. Be careful about social media: posting about a competition or colleagues can breach the Code's requirements on political impartiality and confidentiality. Honesty on application forms matters: false statements can lead to withdrawal of an offer or disciplinary action. If asked to do something that conflicts with the Code, such as altering a score for a friend, raise it through the Code routes. If you are unsure, ask HR or your line manager before you act, because it is easier to prevent a problem than to fix it.

items.title: L15: Interpreting mixed feedback and changing course
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: Feedback from several competitions can point in different directions, and a skilled candidate treats it as data to be interpreted, not a verdict. Suppose your sift scores are strong but you fail interviews, and interview feedback says your answers lacked outcomes in one competition and lacked structure in another. Look for the common factor: perhaps you describe actions well but under-sell results, or you speak too long without a clear shape. Suppose the feedback conflicts: one panel says your evidence was strong on Leadership, another says it was thin. Consider whether the examples differed, whether the level of the post differed, or whether the criteria were weighted differently. Do not average the feedback; ask what would explain both. Suppose your feedback is consistent but you disagree with it: take a second view from a trusted colleague, and test whether the point holds up. Distinguish three types of cause: evidence, where you lack the experience, delivery, where you have it but present it poorly, and fit, where the post or profession is not the right target. Evidence problems need new experience, which takes time, delivery problems need practice, which is quick, and fit problems need a change of aim. Weigh the cost of change: switching profession may reset your evidence, but persisting in a poor fit wastes time. Choose one change, run it for several applications and compare the results, because changing too many things at once hides what worked. Decide a review point, such as six months or after four applications. If your results improve, continue; if not, revisit the diagnosis and seek an outside view. Keep a record so that you can see progress, which is itself encouraging.

items.title: L15: Choosing between a loan, acting up and a lateral move
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Suppose you are an HEO aiming for SEO within two years and you have three opportunities: a six-month loan to another department in a policy role, an acting-up opportunity in your own team at SEO for nine months, and a lateral move to a permanent HEO post in a larger delivery team. No option is obviously best, so reason through the trade-offs against your target. The acting-up gives you evidence at the target grade in a context you know, and it is probably the strongest single piece of evidence if the work is genuine SEO-level work, but it is temporary, may depend on one manager's view and gives no permanent status. The loan gives breadth, a new network and perhaps different stakeholders, and it keeps your substantive post, but it may be at HEO level and less obviously relevant, and it takes you away from your usual team. The lateral move gives permanence and a larger scale and may expose you to more management, but it could delay promotion if it resets your evidence or requires time to learn. Ask: where would your evidence be strongest in a year? Which gives the most visibility to people who will sit on panels? Which carries the least risk if the arrangement ends unexpectedly? Would the acting-up be selected fairly, and does the manager commit to an end date and a recorded assessment? Would the loan include SEO-level duties? Can you combine, for example by acting up first and then taking a loan? The best choice is usually the one that provides recent, higher-grade evidence soon, preserves options and fits your situation. If options are close, consider fit and wellbeing, because a role you can sustain is better than one that burns you out. Whatever you choose, plan how you will capture the evidence from the start.

items.title: L15: Writing a fair reference and supporting a colleague's move
items.source: Civil Service Code; ACAS guidance on references
items.body: Managers regularly write references and provide supporting statements for staff who apply for jobs inside and outside the Civil Service, and the way they do it affects the fairness of the competition and their own integrity. A reference should be accurate, fair and based on evidence the writer has seen. Include facts such as dates, role and duties, and an honest assessment of strengths and areas for development relevant to the post, using examples. Do not exaggerate to help the person leave, and do not understate to keep them. A reference that is misleading can lead to legal claims by either the individual or the new employer, because the writer owes a duty of care to take reasonable care that it is true, accurate and not misleading. Respect confidentiality and data protection: do not include health information or personal matters that are not relevant, and avoid details of disciplinary matters unless the department's policy allows it and the facts are established. Use consistent standards for everyone: a manager who writes glowing references for favourites and cautious ones for others creates unfairness. In internal competitions, references are typically taken after a conditional offer and are not used to score candidates, so a manager should not lobby the panel. If a manager is asked for an informal view by a panel member, they should decline and refer the request to the proper process. If you are asked for a reference by someone you have concerns about, you may decline, or give a short factual reference if policy allows, but discuss the matter with HR. When the person is leaving for a promotion, support them and plan the handover; this is part of building a reputation as a good manager. A manager who blocks a legitimate move to retain a good person acts against the person's interests and may breach the department's policies.
